strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem in open-domain tabular QA: retrieving relevant tables from large corpora without dataset-specific fine-tuning.
The coarse-to-fine cascade is intuitive and modular: SPLADE provides high-recall filtering, all-mpnet-base-v2 performs semantic refinement, and text-embedding-3-small handles final reranking.
Retrieval performance is competitive with strong fine-tuned systems: CRAFT obtains R@10 of 87.16 and R@50 of 96.84, exceeding THYME on these metrics while using no NQ-Tables-specific training.
Stage-wise ablations consistently show incremental gains, supporting the value of each retrieval stage.
The paraphrasing experiment suggests strong robustness: even using the reported figures, CRAFT degrades far less than DTR models under query perturbation.

End-to-end experiments with several open-weight LLMs show that CRAFT retrieval can outperform prior retrieval systems when the same generator is used, which is the most compelling evidence for the retrieval contribution.

The appendix includes prompts, retrieval cutoffs, benchmark statistics, configuration details, few-shot analyses, and token-count comparisons, which partially support reproduction and further analysis.
weaknesses: Several central claims are overstated or unsupported. The abstract claims better performance than SOTA hybrid retrievers, but CRAFT underperforms THYME on R@1 and average recall. The text also states that a score of 50.26 surpasses LI-RAGE at 54.17, which is numerically false.

Table 4 is not a fully controlled comparison because CRAFT uses much larger instruction-tuned models, such as 70B/72B LLMs, while several published baselines use different and often weaker generators. The controlled comparison in Table 3 is stronger evidence.

The technical contribution is primarily integrative rather than conceptual: cascaded retrieval, sparse first-stage retrieval, dense reranking, LLM query decomposition, and LLM table summarization are all established techniques.
Evaluation is limited to NQ-Tables. Although the authors acknowledge this, the method's generalizability to other table corpora, domains, languages, or table layouts remains unverified.

Reproducibility is weakened by dependence on proprietary Gemini and OpenAI APIs. The paper does not clearly state that code, generated table descriptions, sub-questions, paraphrases, random seeds, or cached API outputs will be released; closed-model outputs may also change over time.

The efficiency evaluation is incomplete. Generating descriptions for 169,898 tables with Gemini may be expensive, and the paper reports no end-to-end latency, monetary cost, memory use, or runtime comparison against baselines. Token savings from mini-tables do not account for cascade or preprocessing overhead.

Some methodological details are underspecified, including how rows are selected for mini-tables, how table and row embeddings are aggregated into a table score, how cutoffs were chosen, and how generated descriptions were validated.
The evaluation setup around 919 versus 966 test queries is confusing and could affect comparability with reported baselines. The paper should state exactly which queries were used for every result.

There is no statistical-significance testing or variance analysis. Robustness is evaluated using paraphrases from only one Gemini model, without human quality checks or alternative perturbation types, and possible benchmark contamination by proprietary models is not discussed.

Presentation and consistency need improvement: model names and sizes differ across the methodology and tables, few-shot benefits are described inconsistently between the main text and appendix, and at least one reported average change in Table 2 appears inconsistent with the underlying scores.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: scalable open-domain table retrieval and QA without task-specific fine-tuning.
The empirical evaluation covers sparse, dense, and hybrid retrievers and includes stage-wise ablations, query-perturbation tests, multiple LLMs, different retrieval depths, and few-shot settings.
The cascaded design shows plausible high-recall behavior: SPLADE provides very high deep-rank recall, while subsequent semantic and neural reranking improve R@10 and R@1.
The perturbation experiment suggests that the full pipeline may be more stable than DTR under automatically generated query paraphrases.
Using only the top five rows per retrieved table substantially reduces prompt length, and the paper provides token-count evidence for this practical trade-off.
The appendix includes the prompts used for table description, query expansion, and answer generation, which partially supports inspection of the method.
weaknesses: Several headline claims are overstated or contradicted by the results. CRAFT underperforms THYME on R@1 (41.13 vs. 48.55), while the paper itself states that THYME has the best average retrieval performance; thus claims of uniformly better retrieval than hybrid SOTA systems are unsupported.

There is a direct numerical contradiction in the end-to-end analysis: the text says a score of 50.26 at n=1 already surpasses LI-RAGE's 54.17, when it does not. Only some larger models at n=5 exceed LI-RAGE.

The claim that five-shot prompting helps across all models and retrieval depths is also contradicted by Table 3: for Llama3, five-shot performance at n=3 and n=5 is substantially worse than zero-shot. The appendix itself acknowledges that in-context examples do not consistently help.

The evaluation setting is not fully comparable. CRAFT is evaluated on 919 unique test queries, whereas at least some baseline results are reported for all 966 test queries. The paper does not clearly reconcile duplicate handling, denominators, or whether all comparisons use the same subset.

Table 4 appears to compare CRAFT with large instruction-tuned models such as Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen2.5-72B against external baselines whose generators, prompts, and model sizes may differ. These comparisons are not controlled and should not be presented as direct evidence of superiority without clarification.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper does not state whether code, generated table titles/descriptions, or Gemini-generated subquestions will be released. It also omits API versions, temperatures, sampling settings, F1 normalization, and monetary or computational costs for the proprietary Gemini and OpenAI components.

Important retrieval details are unspecified: how original queries and subquestions are combined, how scores over titles, headers, cells, and descriptions are aggregated, how the top five rows are selected, how row scores become table scores, and whether dense row scoring is applied corpus-wide or only after SPLADE filtering. Candidate cutoffs also differ across the prose, figure, and tables.

The model naming is confusing. The methodology describes Llama3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B, while Table 4 reports Mistral-Small, Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen2.5-72B, and Llama-3.3-70B without clearly explaining how these experiments relate.

Efficiency and scalability are asserted rather than measured. There is no wall-clock runtime, memory usage, latency, API-call count, or end-to-end cost comparison. Gemini-based preprocessing and two reranking stages may add substantial overhead, and prompt-token reduction alone does not establish retrieval efficiency.
Generalization is evaluated on only one benchmark, NQ-Tables. The claims of adaptability across evolving domains would require validation on additional table retrieval or tabular QA datasets.

The technical novelty is somewhat limited because sparse-to-dense cascading, LLM query expansion, table summarization, and cross-encoder/embedding reranking are all established techniques. The contribution is primarily an empirical integration, making the rigor of the evidence especially important.

The proposed table descriptions do not improve the chosen SPLADE first-stage retriever in Table 6, weakening the claim that generated table descriptions are a central source of gain. The clearer improvements come from query decomposition and later reranking stages.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: open-domain tabular QA without dataset-specific fine-tuning. The modular sparse-to-dense-to-reranker cascade is intuitive and easy to deploy or modify.
Retrieval results on NQ-Tables are strong at deeper ranks, with CRAFT achieving R@10 of 87.16 and R@50 of 96.84, competitive with strong supervised and hybrid systems such as THYME.

The stage-wise ablation is useful: SPLADE provides high-recall candidate generation, the Sentence-Transformer stage improves mid-rank precision, and the neural reranker yields a substantial R@1 improvement.
The perturbation experiment suggests practical robustness to query paraphrasing: CRAFT's average recall degrades much less than the DTR baselines, including variants trained with hard negatives.

The end-to-end evaluation spans several open-weight LLMs and different retrieval depths. With larger instruction-tuned models and five retrieved tables, CRAFT outperforms listed dataset-specific baselines such as RAG, DPR-RAGE, and LI-RAGE.

The sub-table representation provides a practical efficiency benefit, reducing prompt token length by over 70% relative to full-table inputs. Including prompts, dataset statistics, and stage-level ablations also improves transparency.
weaknesses: The central retrieval claim is overstated. CRAFT does not outperform all prior systems at every rank: its R@1 is 41.13, below DPR (45.32), BIBERT+SPLADE (45.62), and THYME (48.55). Its advantages over THYME at R@10 and R@50 are small and are not accompanied by significance tests or confidence intervals.

Some end-to-end claims are inconsistent with the tables. For example, Mistral-Small-Instruct at n=1 scores 50.26 F1 and therefore does not surpass LI-RAGE's 54.17; it only does so at n=5. The main text also claims consistent 5-shot gains, while Table 12 and the appendix show that few-shot prompting can hurt performance, especially for Llama3.

Evaluation is limited to one benchmark, NQ-Tables, with only 919 unique queries used for end-to-end evaluation. Generalization to other table corpora, domains, table sizes, and query distributions remains unestablished.

Reproducibility is only partially adequate. The system depends on proprietary Gemini and OpenAI APIs, but the paper does not provide an artifact link, released generated table descriptions/sub-questions, API parameters, random seeds, embedding-distance/pooling details, serialization/truncation rules, or the source of few-shot examples.

It is unclear how the candidate cutoffs (5,000, 1,000, and 100 tables) and other retrieval choices were selected. If these were chosen using test-set performance rather than the training split, the reported results may be optimistically biased.

Scalability and efficiency claims are not fully supported. The paper reports final-answer token savings but does not measure end-to-end latency, monetary cost, or the substantial preprocessing cost of generating titles and descriptions for 169,898 tables with Gemini.

Several methodological details are ambiguous, especially how rows are selected and scored in Stage 2, how row-level embeddings are converted into table-level scores, and how sub-questions are combined with the original query during reranking.

The conceptual novelty is relatively incremental: cascaded sparse retrieval, dense reranking, neural reranking, query expansion, and LLM answer generation are established techniques. The contribution is primarily an empirical systems integration rather than a new retrieval algorithm.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem in open-domain tabular QA and presents a clear modular sparse-to-dense cascade that combines SPLADE, dense pruning, neural reranking, LLM-generated query/table enrichment, and mini-table construction.

Retrieval results are strong on NQ-Tables, with the final system reaching 49.84 R@1, 86.83 R@10, and 97.17 R@50. It also obtains competitive high-recall zero-shot results on the larger OTT-QA corpus, including 89.88 R@10 and 96.07 R@50 without task-specific fine-tuning.

The end-to-end evaluation in Table 5 is particularly useful because it compares different retrievers under the same three generator LLMs; CRAFT consistently improves F1 across models and retrieval depths. The mini-table representation also substantially reduces context length, often by about 70% or more according to Table 7.

The paper includes useful stage-wise and component ablations for table descriptions, query decomposition, irrelevant-row removal, and neural reranking, along with a query-paraphrasing robustness experiment and qualitative error analyses.

The method is relevant to computational linguistics and NLP, and the appendix provides prompts and model details that improve understandability. The overall framework is practically attractive as a plug-and-play alternative to dataset-specific retriever training.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is mostly incremental: sparse-to-dense cascades, LLM query expansion, generated table metadata, and cross-encoder/embedding reranking are established techniques. The contribution is primarily an engineered integration rather than a new retrieval algorithm or modeling insight.

The strongest NQ-Tables state-of-the-art claim is not fully established statistically. The final gains over THYME are only 1.29 R@1, 0.45 R@10, and 1.09 R@50 on 966 test queries, but there are no confidence intervals, bootstrap tests, repeated runs, or significance analysis. The comparison is also asymmetric because CRAFT uses Gemini-generated enrichment and text-embedding-3-large.

The end-to-end state-of-the-art comparison in Table 6 is not generator-controlled: CRAFT uses newer or larger instruction-tuned models and GPT-4o, whereas the baselines may use different generators. Table 5 provides the cleaner controlled evidence and should be the basis for the strongest claim.

The OTT-QA end-to-end study is conducted in an oracle setting with gold passages, so it does not demonstrate a complete open-domain table-and-passage QA pipeline. The abstract and contribution wording should explicitly distinguish OTT-QA retrieval performance from full end-to-end OTT-QA performance.

Dataset-specific model choices weaken the claimed generalizability: Stage 2 uses all-mpnet-base-v2 for NQ-Tables but Jina Embeddings v3 for OTT-QA, while Stage 3 uses OpenAI embeddings for NQ-Tables and Gemini embeddings for OTT-QA. The paper should specify a development-set selection protocol or report a single non-dataset-specific configuration.

The efficiency analysis is incomplete and potentially misleading. It does not account for the Gemini cost of generating titles and descriptions for 169K/419K tables or per-query sub-questions. The distinction between offline precomputed embeddings, the stated 5,100 mini-table embeddings per query, and online API calls is also unclear. Wall-clock latency, monetary cost, and total token usage should be reported.

Reproducibility is only adequate rather than strong. The submitted manuscript does not show the promised code/data URL, and it lacks release details for the generated table descriptions and sub-queries, API temperatures/versions, random seeds, ANN-index settings, stage cutoff-selection procedure, and the exact row-to-table score aggregation used in Stage 2.

The robustness study uses paraphrases generated by a Gemini model, with one perturbation per question, which may be relatively mild and stylistically close to the same models used in the pipeline. Diverse human paraphrases or multiple perturbation types would be more convincing. The near-duplicate-table issue noted in the error analysis also complicates R@1 evaluation.

Although mini-tables improve efficiency, retaining only the top five rows can remove distributed or multi-hop evidence. This risk is especially relevant for OTT-QA, and the paper would benefit from a more quantitative analysis of recall loss caused by row filtering rather than only downstream F1 and case studies.

strengths: Addresses an important and relevant NLP problem: scalable open-domain retrieval over very large table corpora without dataset-specific fine-tuning.
The modular sparse-to-dense cascade is intuitive and the stage-wise experiments consistently show recall improvements from SPLADE retrieval through dense pruning and final reranking.

Evaluation is broad for a system paper: two benchmarks, several sparse/dense/hybrid baselines, multiple open-source LLMs, few-shot settings, paraphrase robustness, token analysis, ablations, and qualitative error cases.

The reported NQ-Tables retrieval results are strong, with R@1 of 49.84, R@10 of 86.83, and R@50 of 97.17, and the controlled 7B-generator comparisons in Table 5 generally favor CRAFT over the listed retrieval baselines.
Mini-table construction substantially reduces context length, and the reported token reductions plausibly improve downstream LLM efficiency.
The paper includes the main prompts and explicitly acknowledges several scope limitations, including the oracle nature of the OTT-QA end-to-end evaluation.
weaknesses: The headline SOTA comparison is not fully controlled. CRAFT uses Gemini-generated table titles/descriptions, query decomposition, modern embedding models, and mini-table construction, while the compared retrievers do not receive the same LLM-based enrichment. The results show that the full system works, but do not isolate whether the gains come from the cascade or from the additional proprietary semantic enrichment.

The end-to-end SOTA claim based on GPT-4o versus LI-RAGE is confounded by the answer generator: GPT-4o is not paired with the competing retrievers. Table 5 is more credible because it holds 7B generators fixed, but those comparisons lack significance tests or repeated runs.

The OTT-QA end-to-end evaluation is oracle-like because retrieved tables are paired with gold passages. This measures retrieval quality under favorable conditions rather than a complete open-domain table-and-passage QA pipeline, and the abstract's broader open-domain claims are correspondingly overstated. CRAFT also trails THYME by 11.1 points in OTT-QA R@1.

There is a material inconsistency in the canonical model configuration. Table 2 reports CRAFT on NQ-Tables using text-embedding-3-large with R@1 49.84, whereas Table 8 labels the small-model result, R@1 41.13, as CRAFT. The headline SOTA result depends on which configuration is actually the proposed system.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the current version. The code/data URL is blank, the paper alternates between Gemini-1.5-Flash and Gemini-2.5-Flash, candidate cutoffs such as N1 and N2 are not consistently specified, and generation settings such as temperature, seeds, API versions, and failure handling are not fully documented.

The efficiency analysis is incomplete. It largely ignores the offline cost of using Gemini to generate titles and descriptions for 169,898 or 419,183 tables, as well as indexing and pre-embedding costs. The statement about 33x fewer online embeddings also coexists with contradictory wording about precomputed row embeddings versus 5,100 mini-table embeddings generated per query; no wall-clock latency or monetary cost is reported.

The technical contribution is primarily an engineering integration of known components: sparse-to-dense cascades, LLM query expansion, LLM table summarization, bi-encoder reranking, and context compression. The paper would benefit from a clearer distinction between no task-specific fine-tuning and reliance on large proprietary models.

Use of Gemini and OpenAI models raises possible benchmark contamination and external-knowledge confounds, especially because Gemini directly inspects tables and queries to produce retrieval-enabling text. This risk is not analyzed.

The evaluation is concentrated mainly on single-hop NQ-Tables and an oracle OTT-QA setting, so evidence for genuine multi-hop reasoning, synthesis across multiple tables and passages, and deployment to new domains remains limited.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, modular cascade that combines sparse retrieval, dense pruning, neural reranking, mini-table construction, and LLM-based answer generation without dataset-specific fine-tuning.
Retrieval results are strong on NQ-Tables, with reported R@1/R@10/R@50 of 49.84/86.83/97.17, and the system remains competitive at high recall depths on the larger OTT-QA corpus.

The evaluation is broad: it covers two benchmarks, several open and proprietary LLMs, varying numbers of retrieved tables, zero- and few-shot prompting, paraphrase robustness, stage-wise ablations, token reduction, and qualitative error analysis.

The mini-table representation is practically useful: retaining only selected rows substantially shortens downstream contexts and is shown in several settings to preserve or improve answer F1 while reducing irrelevant evidence.
The paper includes detailed prompts and model choices and promises code and generated artifacts, which supports reproducibility despite its reliance on external APIs.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily architectural and empirical: cascaded retrieval, LLM-generated query/table enrichment, sparse-to-dense reranking, and context compression are already established ideas, and the paper does not introduce a substantially new retrieval algorithm.

The 'training-free' and efficiency claims need qualification. Generating table descriptions and query expansions with Gemini Flash over hundreds of thousands of tables incurs substantial offline API cost, and the 33× embedding reduction is compared with a brute-force dense setup rather than a standard precomputed dense ANN index.

The primary final reranker is reported inconsistently: the headline NQ-Tables SOTA score uses text-embedding-3-large, while the main pipeline description, efficiency analysis, and Table 8 appear to use text-embedding-3-small, whose R@1 is much lower at 41.13. The main configuration and corresponding cost/latency should be clarified.
The NQ-Tables improvements over THYME are small and no significance tests, variance estimates, or repeated API runs are provided. This makes it difficult to judge whether the gains are stable.

OTT-QA end-to-end QA is evaluated only in an oracle setting in which retrieved tables are paired with gold passages, so the paper does not demonstrate a complete open-domain OTT-QA system. Its R@1 on OTT-QA is also substantially below the supervised THYME result.

Reproducibility is weakened by the blank artifact link and dependence on proprietary, version-sensitive APIs. Exact generation parameters, API versions, temperatures, and released generated table descriptions/query expansions should be provided.

Robustness testing is limited to paraphrases generated by a model from the same Gemini family, with no human validation or diverse perturbation types such as typos, entity ambiguity, or adversarial reformulations.
The paper does not deeply analyze hallucinated or misleading Gemini-generated descriptions/subqueries, even though these components could introduce bias or propagate errors before retrieval begins.
